The white redhorse sucker Catostomus commersonii is a demersal freshwater fish native to eastern North America. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0056 grams [Wwb = 0.0056 grams], a value consistent with the minute, yolk-absorbing prolarvae typical of catostomids. These lecithotrophic individuals undergo rapid yolk resorption before transitioning to exogenous feeding. Mature adults in this species can attain an ultimate total length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of the sucker family. The pronounced size range from the tiny hatchling to the large adult reflects a growth strategy common among iteroparous teleosts that invest little per offspring but compensate through high fecundity over a long reproductive lifespan. Gravid fish are frequently observed in spring spawning runs, where they deposit adhesive demersal eggs over gravel substrates.

The onset of gonadal activity in Catostomus commersonii is closely tied to body size rather than strictly to chronological age. Field surveys indicate that individuals reach sexual maturation at a total length of approximately 23 centimeters [Lp = approximately 23 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds more reliably with the transition to reproductive viability than does a fixed age. At this body length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated at 148.5 grams [Wwp = 148.5 grams], derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The delay in maturation until a substantial body size is attained is a typical pattern among catostomids, likely linked to the need for sufficient somatic gape and swimming performance to exploit seasonally abundant food resources during the energetically demanding spawning period. This size-based puberty allows individuals to maximize lifetime reproductive output.

Reproductive output in the white redhorse sucker has been modeled based on the fecundity of the closely related Moxostoma valenciennesi. Under a thermal regime of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], females produce approximately 5,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5,000 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately 10 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 10 times per year], yielding a substantial annual fecundity that reflects the typical iteroparous strategy of a species that ascends tributaries annually. The reliance on high fecundity compensates for the relatively small size of each egg and the vulnerability of the pelagic-larval phase. Spawning adults ascend tributaries in early spring, and the incubation period is temperature-dependent, with the yolk-sac alevin stage being particularly sensitive to thermal fluctuations during the period of organogenesis and early development.

As individuals continue to grow past the puberty stage, they eventually approach their ultimate adult size, which is associated with a substantial increase in body mass. The maximum recorded wet weight of an adult white redhorse sucker is 3320 grams [Wwi = 3320 grams], corresponding to the fish that have reached the asymptotic length of 65 centimeters. This ultimate mass represents a considerable investment in somatic tissue, supporting the migratory and reproductive activities of the species. In terms of lifespan, these fish are relatively long-lived for a freshwater catostomid; the maximum recorded longevity in the wild is approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extended lifespan allows individuals to participate in many spawning seasons. The long life is achieved under the seasonal thermal conditions of temperate streams, with a typical annual temperature cycle, and the species has been documented to live this long at an average annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

The ecological context of the white redhorse sucker's life history reveals a demographic strategy that balances early investment in somatic growth with delayed but sustained reproduction. The substantial difference between the 148.5 gram [Wwp = 148.5 gram] mass at puberty and the ultimate adult mass of over three kilograms underscores the extended period of somatic growth that occurs after sexual maturation in this species. This prolonged growth phase, observed across numerous field studies in the Great Lakes and upper Mississippi drainages, allows individuals to increase their reproductive output with age, as larger females are known to produce not only more eggs per spawning event but also to spawn more frequently during the spring migration. Compared to shorter-lived cypriniforms such as Pimephales promelas, which may complete their life cycle within a single year, Catostomus commersonii exemplifies a slower-paced strategy with high annual fecundity and a maximum size of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters] that is among the largest recorded for North American catostomids.
